title: The Enlightenment

cards.b:
In 1784 the German philosopher Immanuel Kant answered a magazine's question, 'What is Enlightenment?' His answer: it is humans leaving behind their self-imposed laziness in thinking. His motto was Sapere aude, 'Dare to know'.

That daring changed kings, churches and the way we vote.

The Enlightenment (roughly the late 1600s to the late 1700s) grew out of the Scientific Revolution. If reason can explain the planets, why not government, religion and trade?

Ideas travelled in coffeehouses, salons hosted by clever women in Paris, and print. The huge Encyclopedie of Diderot (1751-72) tried to gather all knowledge.

John Locke (Two Treatises, 1689): people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and can remove a ruler who breaks the trust. Montesquieu (The Spirit of the Laws, 1748): separate the powers of government.

Voltaire fought for tolerance and attacked religious persecution, after the Calas affair (1762), in which an innocent Protestant was executed. Rousseau (The Social Contract, 1762) wrote that man is born free but is everywhere in chains, and argued rule should follow the 'general will'.

Rousseau and Voltaire disliked each other intensely.

Adam Smith, in The Wealth of Nations (1776), argued free markets create wealth. Mary Wollstonecraft wrote A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) and said women need education to be equal.

Most Enlightenment writers did not extend 'all men' to women.

Some rulers, called 'enlightened despots', used reason to reform without sharing power: Frederick the Great of Prussia, Catherine the Great of Russia, Joseph II of Austria.

Ideas also lit the revolutions in America and France.

cards.h: Did Voltaire say 'I disapprove of what you say...'?
cards.b:
Myth: Voltaire said, 'I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.'Fact: that line was written in 1906 by Evelyn Beatrice Hall, summing up his attitude. He never wrote it.

Also, many Enlightenment thinkers held racist views or profited from slavery. Historians argue whether those ideas were part of the Enlightenment or a betrayal of it.

Five things to remember

  1. Enlightenment thinkers prized reason and evidence.
  2. Locke: natural rights; Montesquieu: separation of powers.
  3. Voltaire: tolerance; Rousseau: general will.
  4. Smith and Wollstonecraft brought economics and women's rights in.
  5. Ideas had limits: slavery and empire.

Think about it

  • Which Enlightenment idea matters most to you today?
  • Can ideas of freedom be applied unequally?
